name: Bengaluru fort heritage walk
description: Discover the history of the Bengaluru fort on this walk. The Fort though today reduced to a mere fraction of its original expanse—less than 5%—remains one of the most significant remnants of the city’s pre-colonial past. This heritage walk invites you to step into the vestiges of a fort that once bore witness to battles transitions of power architectural ingenuity and political resilience.The fort began as a modest mud structure before being fortified with stone during Hyder Ali’s rule and later expanded under his son Tipu Sultan. These walls though weathered by time preserve within them the layered narratives of a growing urban center and the complexities of South Indian resistance to British expansion.A highlight of the walk is the iconic Tipu Sultan’s Summer Palace a rare example of Indo-Islamic architecture with its intricate wooden pillars frescoes and elegant symmetry. Once the seat of royal administration and leisure the palace offers insights not only into architectural aesthetics but also into the socio-political life of the Sultanate in the 18th century.As we navigate the narrow lanes of Old Bengaluru one encounters a little-known but historically important site: a surviving armoury tucked into the urban sprawl and forgotten by modern maps. Used during Tipu’s reign this structure is a physical testament to the city’s martial past and the strategic importance of Bangalore in Mysore’s military planning.A focal point of this walk is the Battle of Bangalore (1791) a critical campaign during the Third Anglo-Mysore War. The battle pitted the British East India Company against Tipu Sultan’s forces and highlighted not only the military prowess of the Sultanate but also broader geopolitical shifts—especially the fallout of British actions in other global theatres such as in the American Revolutionary War.It is particularly notable that the Mysorean rockets used innovatively during this time caught the attention of British military observers. Some of these designs later found their way into documentation that would influence the development of European—and even American—military technology. Legend holds that they partly inspired Francis Scott Key’s reference to "the rockets' red glare" in the Star-Spangled Banner.Finally the walk concludes with a return to the present—by way of South Indian culinary tradition offering participants a curated local snack and a cup of filter coffee. A reminder that history does not only reside in books or ruins—it lives on in tastes traditions and memories.This walking tour is not just about stones and structures. It is a curated window into Bengaluru’s transformation—from fortified stronghold and seat of regional power to colonial outpost and finally to modern metropolis. In walking its paths we do not merely observe history; we retrace it.Note : "This walk is led by a Bengaluru native and professional architect who has lived and studied in the vicinity of the fort for over three decades. His deep-rooted connection to the area combined with his architectural expertise gives him an intimate knowledge of not just every corner of the fort but also the rich history that surrounds it."

name: Nagarathpete heritage walk.
description: This is what I post about the walk for marketing...On the fourth of our walks through Kempe Gowda’s historic *Pettah*, we venture into one of the oldest and most fascinating quarters of Bengaluru, where centuries of history continue to unfold through its narrow, meandering lanes.Our walk begins with a darshan at one of the city’s most beloved temples, intimately associated with Bengaluru’s celebrated Karaga festival. From here, we wander deeper into the Pettah, uncovering forgotten monuments, old neighbourhoods and stories concealed behind the façades of modern Bengaluru.Along the way, we discover the remarkable story of Mysore’s rockets—military technology perfected under Tipu Sultan and manufactured in this very part of the city. We explore how these rockets travelled from the battlefields of Mysore to Britain, and ultimately influenced the technology that inspired the words of the American national anthem.The walk then takes us to a site connected with India’s struggle for independence, before offering a glimpse into one of the Pettah’s enduring traditions: its silk-weaving community.And, time permitting, we make a quiet visit to the tombs of Sufi warriors who were martyred during the Third Anglo-Mysore War of 1791, adding another, lesser-known chapter to the layered history of the neighbourhood.This is a walk through a Bengaluru that is easy to miss—a city of temples and tombs, warriors and weavers, rockets and revolutionaries, where history survives in lanes, workshops and places of worship.Come walk with us and discover the Pettah beyond the postcard. Spaces are limited, so book your place and join us for this journey into the hidden history of old Bengaluru.

name: Kalighat Painting Workshop
description: KALIGHAT PAINTINGS – WHERE TRADITION MEETS MODERNITYBengal is renowned for its rich cultural heritage and diverse artistic traditions, including music, literature, dance, and visual arts. In this workshop, we will explore one of Bengal's most fascinating and thought-provoking art forms—Kalighat Paintings.Bold, expressive & vibrant, Kalighat paintings beautifully bring together a variety of themes, ranging from Hindu mythology and spirituality to secular life and social commentary.Originating in 19th-century Kolkata during the colonial period, this distinctive art form developed around the Kalighat Temple, dedicated to Goddess Kali. The paintings were traditionally created on patas (cloth or paper scrolls) by artists known as Patuas. Located near the banks of the Hooghly River and the popular Kalighat Temple, the area attracted pilgrims, locals, and foreign visitors, creating a thriving audience for these unique artworks.However, with the growing popularity of printed reproductions in the early 20th century, traditional handmade Kalighat paintings gradually declined.The legacy of this expressive art form was later reinterpreted and celebrated by renowned Indian artist Jamini Roy, who drew inspiration from Bengal's folk traditions and brought a distinctive modern interpretation to traditional Indian art.What will you learn?Learn about the history and evolution of Kalighat PaintingsExplore the life and artistic journey of Jamini RoyUnderstand the distinctive themes, styles, and visual language of this art formDiscover how traditional Indian folk art influenced modern artistic expressionCreate your very own Kalighat-inspired paintingThis will be a wonderful opportunity to experience Indian art and culture through storytelling, learning, and hands-on creativity!Note:All art materials required for the workshop will be provided by the host.What will you take home?A Detailed Hands-On Workshop WorkbookKnowledge & History of Kalighat art & cultureYour very own completed artwork created during the workshopWhat do you need to bring?A water bottle to keep yourself hydrated.All workshop materials will be provided. However, if preferred, you may bring an examination pad or paper board for additional support while working.Please NoteKindly be on time, Participants arriving late may miss the storytelling and introduction to the history of this beautiful art form.No refunds will be provided for cancellations.Come, explore the vibrant world of Kalighat Paintings, where storytelling, tradition, culture, and creativity come together & take home a beautiful piece of art created by you!

name: Mycelium and Muse - Interactive Science Class
description: We often equate creativity with making art. Picasso was creative. Beethoven was creative. Van Gogh was creative.But what about the person who first picked up a piece of charcoal and scribbled on the wall of a cave, hoping the people in the next cave would get the message? Or the bowerbird who spends an entire season collecting blue bottle caps and flowers to decorate a little stage for a mate?And what about a fungus? This one is literally brainless, yet it sends out electrical signals that, when connected to a synthesizer, play out like music.So if creativity shows up in organisms without brains, it is far older than us, isn't it? That's the question we'll sit with over coffee: where creativity really begins on the tree of life, and what that means for those of us who have spent years saying "I'm just not the creative type."Along the way, you'll hear a mushroom play music, and you'll make something that is deliberately, wonderfully bad. You don't need any science background to join in.Just come, grab a coffee, and let's get some creativity brewing. Because, tell you what, I'm not sure a creative life is a happier one. But I'm pretty sure it's a far more meaningful one.About the Speaker:Bitasta Datta is a microbiologist by training, an educator by profession and a science storyteller by passion.For over 10 years, she has been turning science into stories for school learners and curious adults. She started at the National Digital Library of India, went on to co-found The Synapse, led curriculum and learning experience design at BYJU'S and Tutopiya, and tinkers with content at Khan Academy.

name: Bhima
description: BhimaSunday, 22nd November, 6.00 p.m. - 7.10 p.m.Language: EnglishAbout the PerformanceDrawing inspiration from Ashok Malhotra’s Child Man, MT Vasudevan Nair’s Randamoozham, and Jeanette Winterson’s Weight, this play explores the paradoxes and ironies in the life of the second Pandava, Bhima.Who is Bhima? What is his hunger? Who feeds it? What are the choices available to a hero? What is the fate of a strong man in contemporary times? These are some of the questions around which the key narrative of the play evolves. What is his relevance to contemporary life? Would his version of masculinity be acceptable in today’s world?If Bhima were to live today, who would he be — a loyal middle-management warrior who is the engine of the company but never its CEO? A family man who defines himself only in terms of roles — the breadwinner, the husband, the son — who will do anything for his family? Or does he exist as an individual beyond these roles? Does society look after its Bhimas, or is it only Arjuna we want?Contrasting the Koodiyattam form with contemporary dialogue and commentary, using music and poetry as interventions, Bhima re-examines a version of masculinity and its interaction with modernity.Bhima won the Best Innovative Sound Design award for Sachin Gurjale at the 2017 Mahindra Excellence in Theatre Awards (META).Cast Devised and performed by: Vivek Vijayakumaran and Sachin GurjaleCrewConcept: Vivek VijayakumaranDirection: Anitha SanthanamText: Sachin Gurjale, Vivek Vijayakumaran, Ajith Lal, Swetanshu Bora and Anitha SanthanamCostume: Surabhi Vasisht and Aruna MPoster Design: Pratyush SinghLighting Designer: Manju NarayanProduction Manager: Robin JoeAbout the ArtistsVivek VijayakumaranVivek Vijayakumaran is a Bengaluru-based theatre director, actor, and pedagogue with over 15 years of experience in performance, embodied research, and actor training. Trained under masters including Heisnam Kanhailal, Guru G. Venu, and at the Workcenter of Jerzy Grotowski and Thomas Richards, his practice integrates traditional Indian performance frameworks like Navarasa with contemporary physical theatre. His paper on his pedagogy of training contemporary actors in Navarasas has been selected for publication.As Artistic Director of Our Theatre Collective and Studio, Vivek leads experimental, research-driven performance initiatives. His original stage work includes directing the contemporary physical theatre piece The Thumb and acclaimed productions like IT IS YOU. He has acted in the feature film, Pada. Vivek has served as visiting faculty at Drama School Mumbai and Azim Premji University, and trained over 300 performers in India. He was named one of Forbes India’s 12 Boundary-Pushing Theatre Innovators.Sachin GurjaleSachin Gurjale is a theatre practitioner, drummer and sound designer and has been active in the Bengaluru cultural scene for over two decades. Sachin’s collaboration in the Bhima project dates back to 2014 when he travelled with Vivek to Iranjalakuda to study the role of the Mizhavu in a Koodiyattam performance under the guidance of Kalamandalam Rajeev. With this perspective, he designed a percussive score for Bhima that brought his own influence of the African djembe and other urban folk instruments.Anitha SanthanamAnitha Santhanam is a seasoned theatre and movement practitioner based in Bengaluru. Holding the embodied imagination as its core, her creative work spans performance, direction and teaching. She was part of the core faculty team at Drama School Mumbai (2022-2024), faculty of Integral Theatre on the FECAT program at SMART (2013-2022) and an artist-in-residence at the Srishti Manipal institute of Art, Design and Technology Bengaluru (2009-2013).Anitha is also a two-time awardee of the Charles Wallace India Trust scholarship through which she trained in actor-created theatre and the Lecoq pedagogy at LISPA London, under the mentorship of Thomas Pratkki.During her time in London, Anitha also trained with ARTIS education to facilitate integrated arts-in-education programs in schools and with JABADAO in developmental movement play for children. She is a trained Bharatanatyam performer and holds a diploma in Choreography from NIKC, Bengaluru.Photo Credits: Bharath TiwariAbout the FestivalPLAYINTERPLAY is a theatre festival with a difference. It celebrates 50 years of the Inlaks Shivdasani Foundation, bringing together its theatre awardees and scholars to show their work, share their experiences, skills and learnings, and converse on matters of common interest.PLAYINTERPLAY presents plays that are new to Bengaluru. What is different, however, is that it looks back as well as forward, featuring a work of theatre that has been specially revived for the festival and readings of plays that are still to become the finished article.PLAYINTERPLAY does more: it forges connections between its constituent parts — performances, workshops, conversations and experience sharing — emphasising the interplay between thought, learning and practice.See the plays! Apply for the workshops! Join the conversations! Soak in the magic of theatre.About the Artistic Director Anmol Vellani is the founder and former executive director of India Foundation for the Arts, the first independent philanthropic organisation in India devoted exclusively to supporting the arts. He is also the co-founder of Toto Funds the Arts, which nurtures, encourages and rewards new voices and emerging talent in the arts.Anmol did not, however, aspire to become a professional in the field of philanthropy. His early fascination was with the arts, especially theatre and music, and also philosophy, which he studied at the Universities of Poona, Oxford and Cambridge. He taught ethics, logic and the history of philosophy at Elphinstone College, Mumbai, in the 1970s.His writing and talks — on arts entrepreneurship, the creative economy, cultural policy, the role of grant-making foundations, culture and development, arts collaboration and the performing arts, for example — have reflected on the insights he has gleaned from his long engagement with the arts and philanthropy.Anmol has been associated with nearly 50 plays as a director, designer or actor. He has directed theatre productions in different languages and cities. His last two plays — Innocence (2024) and Apne Ghar Jaisa (2022) — have been lauded for their sharp and critical look at contemporary social and political realities in India.

name: The Death of Galileo
description: The Death of GalileoWednesday, 25th November, 7.30 p.m. - 8.50 p.m.Language: HindiAbout the PerformanceThis play is an adaptation of Bertolt Brecht’s Life of Galileo. Using a non-linear theatrical structure, it connects Galileo’s struggle to contemporary realities.The play unfolds at night inside a museum, where a group arrives to demolish its collection of cultural and collective living memories and objects. Among the artefacts, they discover a telescope, which becomes the point of departure for the story of Galileo — his discoveries, struggles, confinement and unceasing search for truth. As the night progresses, Galileo’s time and the present time begin to unfold simultaneously, revealing parallels between social realities in two different historical moments.The members of the demolition group are themselves caught between disillusionment, violence and self-deception. Their encounter with the museum and with Galileo stirs their conscience, and while one group remains adamant, the other begins to question its reasons for wanting to destroy the museum. An internal conflict begins, between the path they’ve chosen, to raze the museum for their pride, and the path their conscience wants to guide them towards. Experimental music anchors the play in the present moment, voicing the characters' contradictions and a call to act for co-existence.The performance draws on Brecht’s distancing effect alongside character expression, an actor-development process emerging from Rajkumar Rajak’s research.CastGalileo Galilei: Ramratan GugaliaAndrea and Roman Pope: Mohit VaishnavVihan and Barberini (Narrator): Adnan KhanYoginder and Hitler: Aftab NoorVijay and Sipahi: Ashish DhapBalveer and Roman Sanyasi: Chitaranjan NamaDhyan and Astronomer: Karan Kumar and Shubham MeghwanshiBruno and Ludovico: Aman TaseraBruno’s Mother and Hamid’s Mother: Raina Raha RajakPeople of Rome and Chorus: Rajwanti Tamoli, Vijaylaxmi Tasera, Niana Raha, Ayush KesarwaniCrewDirector: Rajkumar RajakMusic Design and Composition: Garvit GidwaniMusic Assistants: Aman Tasera, Chitaranjan Nama and Harmendra SartaajLighting Design and Operation: Ravi Kumar Pathak and Harmendra SartaajCostume Design: Shubham Meghwanshi, Raina Raha Rajak and Aftab NoorProps Design: Firoz AlamProduction Managers: Raina Raha and MohitProduction Supervision: Ajeet BahadurProduced by: Ex-tra An Organisation and Community Theatre TonkAbout the ArtistsRajkumar RajakRajkumar Rajak is a theatre artist whose practice connects theatre with education and with communities. description: Goonj ka GharThursday, 26th November, 7.30 p.m. - 8.20 p.m.Language: Hindi (with subtitles in English)About the PerformanceGoonj ka Ghar is a physical theatre performance that combines movement, minimal set design, and fragmented storytelling to explore themes of identity, power, and marginalisation. Initially inspired by three seminal short stories, Tirichh by Uday Prakash, Toba Tek Singh by Saadat Hasan Manto, and Uljhan by Vijaydan Detha, which are woven into a single theatrical narrative that interrogates unresolved questions of identity, belonging and justice in today’s world.Set against the backdrop of a society grappling with citizenship, identity and social justice, the performance raises urgent questions: What makes a person a citizen? What do we call home when borders both physical and psychological remain in flux? Who is considered sane, worthy, beautiful, or legitimate? Why does society continue to value women who appear silent and submissive? description: Kadambari: Tracing Fragments of a Shattered MuseFriday, 27th November, 7.30 p.m - 9.00 p.m.Language: Hindi, BengaliAbout the PerformanceKadambari is a lyrical theatrical journey into the silenced life of Kadambari Devi, Rabindranath Tagore’s critic, muse, companion, and sister-in-law, married into the Tagore household at nine and gone by 25, when the poet himself was only 23. Rather than reducing her to a footnote in his biography, the play seeks to restore her voice, weaving memory, fiction and imagination. It traces fragments of her existence beyond whispers of scandal and tragedy, asking how history chooses to remember or erase the women who stand behind celebrated men.Set during her final hours, the play imagines Death arriving to claim her. As their work as directors and actors has also extended beyond physical theatre, they will reflect on the reasons for their divergent artistic choices.Physical theatre has many strengths. Most notably, it can overcome language barriers, express what words cannot, connect with audiences at a visceral level, harness the ideas and creativity of the whole group, and rely on minimalist scenography. Her partner’s search takes him far beyond Earth, where time unsettles everything they believed they knew about love, duty, and family. When their paths cross again, each has lived differently and in different references of time since the separation. How should they now understand their obligations to one another?Against this story, Juno 77 asks questions at the heart of moral philosophy. Does an intention matter more than its consequences? Can someone be held to a promise in circumstances no one could have imagined? What does it mean to forgive a person whose absence has shaped your entire life?The play also considers how religion helps us live with such questions. Faith offers ways to think about time, sacrifice, suffering and the possibility of reunion. Yet those ideas can mean different things to people who have endured the same loss differently. Bringing space science into conversation with religious thought, Juno 77 asks how we make moral choices when our shared understanding of a life has come apart. It seeks to examine the question of whether our loves and losses are meaningful or mere coincidence.Written and directed by Abhishek Majumdar, the play will be produced by Nalanda Arts Studio in Kannada and Hindustani versions.The Archive on the Wall By Meghna Roy ChoudhuryThe Archive on the Wall is a science fiction play inspired by holographic principle theory that explores memory, scientific thought, and political erasure, set inside a crumbling flat in contemporary Mumbai.After her mother’s death, Aparna, a physicist turned archivist, returns to her childhood home to sort through her belongings. name: How Not to Build a Theatre Institution
description: How Not to Build a Theatre InstitutionA Conversation with Abhishek Mudgal, Sanyukta Saha and Abhishek Majumdar, moderated by Priyanka Varma Friday, 27th November, 5.00 p.m. - 6.30 p.m.About the ConversationArtists establish and lead theatre institutions (which include long-standing initiatives) for different reasons — to practice, teach, present, advocate or support the art form, for instance.But such undertakings, especially if they function independently of secure government or corporate largesse, can falter or fail. The poverty of infrastructure and support for the theatre are among the external factors that are adduced for the precariousness of artist-led institutions. Internal factors are rarely cited. What if the institution is over-reliant on personal equations and goodwill for its sustenance? Or if its ownership is narrowly concentrated in one or two charismatic personalities? Or if it is too obsessed with legacy concerns to avert obsolescence in a swiftly changing environment?This session will investigate what might lie inside any theatre institution that could threaten its stability and hamper its growth. Reflecting on their personal experience of founding and running institutions, three theatre artists will tell us about what worked or did not work about the choices they made. Were discontents allowed to simmer, tensions swept under the carpet or challenges left unaddressed? In hindsight, do they regret any missteps or wish they had done some things differently?About the Participants Sanyukta SahaSanyukta Saha is a theatre pedagogue, facilitator and community arts leader, and the Founder and Executive Director of Aagaaz Theatre Trust, a community-rooted arts organisation in New Delhi. name: Tradition and Modernity in Contemporary Theatre
description: Tradition and Modernity in Contemporary Theatre A Conversation with Sharanya Ramprakash, Laya N Kumar and Parshathy J Nath, moderated by Lakshmana KP Saturday, 28th November, 4.30 p.m. - 6.00 p.m.About the ConversationThe traditions with which contemporary urban Indian theatre artists can engage are immense, embracing mythologies, folk tales and performances, art and craft objects and practices, festivals and rituals, cuisine, inherited knowledge and skills, and much else besides. At the same time, the distinction between the traditional and the modern is not clearcut. Modern theatre in India has a history that stretches back for over two centuries — long enough to develop its own traditions. Dance forms now regarded as ‘classical’ acquired modern practices of teaching, performance and patronage in the last century.The theatre artists in this session will speak about their idea of tradition and how they have interacted with it in the plays they have written, directed or performed. They will also be invited to discuss ethical and political questions that come to the fore when tradition is brought into contemporary theatre work. Has their work been sensitive to the claim that borrowing from inherited forms of expression can constitute a form of cultural theft or disrespects localised and context-specific creation of value and meaning? How would they negotiate with traditions that have been invented in response to market demands or political pressures? Has their work reconciled with, or has it offered a critical perspective on the feudalism, casteism and gender discrimination embedded in many traditional performances and stories?About the ParticipantsSharanya Ramprakash Sharanya Ramprakash is a Bengaluru-based theatre-maker. She places her work at the intersection of gender, tradition and language. She writes, acts, directs and collaborates with a range of forms, communities and theatre-makers across local, national and international locations. Her work is research-based, collaborative and exploratory. She is a member of the Lincoln Centre Director’s Lab, New York. She is also a recipient of the Shankar Nag Theatre Award 2022.Parshathy J NathParshathy J Nath is a theatre artist based in Bengaluru. Over the last ten years, she has worked with some of the best-known theatre directors in south India, including Prasanna Ramaswamy, Rajiv Krishnan, Vinay Kumar, Nimmy Raphel, Sharanya Ramprakash, Aruna Ganesh Ram, Koumarane Valavane and Sanjeeva Suvarna. She has trained at Adishakti Laboratory for Theatre Art Research, Ninasam and Natanakairali. In 2025, she received a production grant from the India Foundation for Arts, with which she created a solo performance piece called Shoorpanakha: A Search. This production has travelled to different cities and has been performed at The School of Drama and Fine Arts, Kerala, Kerala Sangeetha Nataka Akademi, Ranga Shankara, and BLR Hubba 2025.Laya N KumarLaya Kumar has trained with groups like Indian Ensemble, IAPAR and Bhasha Centre, and with award-winning theatre-makers, including Mahesh Dattani and Gurleen Judge. She has worked as a producer on Naatak Express, a fundraiser festival that brings together over 100 artists to make short plays in 24 hours. description: DramatherapyExperience Sharing by Vardhan DeshpandeSaturday, 28th November, 3.00 p.m. - 4.00 p.m.About the SessionIn this session, Vardhan Deshpande reflects on his journey with Dramatherapy and its possibilities as a practice of healing, expression and transformation.Over the past two-and-a-half years, he has been working with children at risk through Dramatherapy sessions, alongside six months of work with specially-abled children. name: Lecture-Demonstration on the Folk Theatre of Bayalata
description: Experience Sharing by Dr Sahana PinjarLecture-Demonstration on the Folk Theatre of BayalataMonday, 23rd November, 7.00 p.m. - 8.00 p.m.About the SessionDr. Sahana Pinjar will be presenting a live demonstration of the traditional Kannada folk-theatre form of Bayalata through the performance of Girija Kalyana, depicting the divine marriage of Girija (Parvati) and Lord Shiva. The demonstration will showcase the storytelling, acting, dialogue, traditional movements, music, costumes, and theatrical conventions of Bayalata, bringing the story to life for a contemporary audience. The story, written by Dr. Basavaraja Malshati, portrays Girija’s deep devotion and determination to attain Lord Shiva, her penance, and the eventual divine wedding. Through lively characters, expressive acting, traditional music and the energetic style of Bayalata, the narrative unfolds as both a sacred tale and a vibrant theatrical experience. name: Mycelium & Muse: A Science Storytelling Workshop
description: About the Workshop:We often equate creativity with making art. Picasso was creative. Beethoven was creative. Van Gogh was creative.But what about the person who first picked up a piece of charcoal and scribbled on the wall of a cave, hoping the people in the next cave would get the message? Or the bowerbird who spends an entire season collecting blue bottle caps and flowers to decorate a little stage for a mate?And what about a fungus? This one is literally brainless, yet it sends out electrical signals that, when connected to a synthesiser, play out like music.So if creativity shows up in organisms without brains, it is far older than us, isn't it?That's the question we'll sit with: Where does creativity really begin on the tree of life, and what does that mean for all of us who have spent years saying "I'm just not the creative type". Along the way, you'll hear a mushroom playing music, make an idea card that is deliberately, wonderfully bad, write a letter to your future self, and discover a new answer to the question “Am I creative?”You don't need any science background to join in. Just come in, and let's get some creativity brewing.Because, tell you what, we are not sure if a creative life is a happier one. But what we can absolutely guarantee is that it's a far more meaningful one.About the facilitator:Bitasta Datta is a microbiologist by training, an educator by profession and a science storyteller by passion.For over 10 years, she has been turning science into stories for school learners and curious adults. She started at the National Digital Library of India, went on to co-found The Synapse, led curriculum and learning experience design at BYJU'S and Tutopiya, and now leads the efforts at Khan Academy India to narrate science in a way that sticks.She believes science and art are two lenses on the same world, and that if you look through both long enough, you arrive at the same philosophy. So that's what she does. She dissects science to find the art in it, dissects art to find the science in it, and narrates her findings as stories.Outside work, she paints, bakes, and travels, and writes about the places where science, art and philosophy run into each other. Mycelium & Muse began as one of those pieces.

name: Ritu Raga Rang: Seasons through Ragas
description: Ritu Raga Rang: Seasons through RagasThe world of Hindustani classical music has been traditionally linked to the idea of seasons. Ancient Indian scriptures described six distinct seasons or ritus: Vasant (Spring), Grishma (summer), Varsha (monsoon), Sharad (Autumn), Hemant (Pre-Winter) and Shishir (Winter). Each of these seasons bring about different moods and feelings. In this multi-sensory performance, which includes Ragamala paintings and fragrances that evoke the feelings of each season, Nishant will paint portraits of the ritus using ragas and compositions as a canvas. This programme premiered at Stanford University to a warm reception and now comes to Bengaluru for the first time.Nishant is accompanied by Sri Udayaraj Karpur on tabla and Sri Surya Upadhyaya on harmonium.The concert is set in Sabha, a restored 160-year-old building in Shivaji Nagar, an intimate space well suited to a baithak-style evening of khayal.About the artistNishant Panicker is a Hindustani vocalist of the Agra-Atrauli gharana and a disciple of the late Vidushi Lalith J. Rao. He received his early training from the late sarod maestro Pandit Rajeev Taranath. At 15 he was a finalist in Naad Bhed, the national classical music talent search by SPIC MACAY and Doordarshan, and at 18 he was among the youngest recipients of the NCPA Hindustani Vocal Scholarship. He has performed at many prestigious venues across India and USA including the NCPA Mumbai, India International Centre Delhi, Bharat Bhavan Bhopal, Bangalore International Centre, Chowdiah Memorial Hall, Stanford University, Chinmaya Amarnath Pittsburgh and the Chhandayan Center in New York. He is also a regular performer in the music collective Sunaad.Facebook | Youtube | Insta

name: unLecture x Gully Labs Bangalore
description: Five very different conversations. One very curious city.Bangalore, we're here!! And we're bringing you five sessions that go from the psychology of power to the politics of citizenship, from economics that turns everything you thought you knew on its head to robots dreaming of Mars, and poetry that asks what it means to keep feeling things in a world that can be a little too much.We're revisiting one of psychology's most famous experiments, questioning who gets to belong in a democracy, finding out why good intentions can make terrible policies, meeting the robots that could one day assist astronauts, and spending an evening with poetry, power, and pleasure.Basically, a little psychology, a little politics, a little science, and a lot of things to think about long after you leave.31st October: The Stanford Prison Experiment: Who Gave You That Power?Ganga M NairThe experiment lasted six days. The legend got a life sentence. We all know the story of ordinary people given power and what supposedly happened next. But what does the experiment actually tell us about human behaviour? And how does power show up in our group chats, relationships, family lunches, and Monday meetings? Through behavioural psychology, neuroscience, and a few experiments on ourselves, we'll unpack the power dynamics hiding in plain sight.1st November: SIR and the Crisis of Documentary CitizenshipAdil HossainWhat does it mean to belong to a country, and who gets to decide? Looking at the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls through the lens of documentary citizenship, political anthropologist Adil Hossain examines how documents, identity, religion, and ideas of belonging shape who gets recognised as a citizen — and who risks being excluded.14th November: The Counter-Intuitive Economist: Stories About Why Good Intentions Make Bad PolicyAnupam ManurIs a cotton tote really better for the planet than a plastic bag? Are higher prices during a disaster always a bad thing? And why do attempts to cut out middlemen so often fail? Professor Anupam Manur takes us through the economic ideas hiding behind everyday assumptions, using stories that challenge what we think we know. No equations, no jargon, just a few surprises about how the world works.22nd November: VLA Rovers: From Assistive Household Companions to Mars ExplorationPradipta BoseWhat if a robot could understand what you say, see the world around it, and figure out what to do next? From assistive technologies that translate eye movements into actions to intelligent rovers designed for the challenges of space, Prof. Pradipta Bose explores how vision-language-action models are changing the way humans and robots work together — on Earth and potentially on Mars.28th November: Zulmaton ke Daur Mein: An Evening of Poetry, Power, and PleasureNeha MishraWhat is the point of poetry in a world that often seems determined to do without it? From Plato's attempts to banish poetry from his Republic to contemporary attempts to regulate art and literature, this session explores why poetry continues to matter. Through a selection of poems, we'll think about emotion, pleasure, politics, and how reading might help us find our way through the overwhelming despair of our times.Five sessions, five different rabbit holes, and hopefully a whole lot of new questions.Bangalore, come curious. Leave with something to think about.

name: Demystifying the P- word
description: Do you find poetry inaccessible, opaque, difficult to read and appreciate?As the oldest form of literature, right from the oral tradition, poetry has always been the way humans told their stories. From Gilgamesh to Homer, from Kalidasa to Wordsworth, from Neruda to Akhmatova, poetry has brought us tales of love and loss and beauty and war.If you want to explore poetry, learn ways to break it down, understand its nuances, its special code, its peculiar love language, then join us as we run you through a selection of poems that let you develop a set of hacks that you can employ when you read your next poem.Whether you are just curious, a poetry enthusiast still trying to figure it out, or a poet hoping to expand your writing horizon, there is something here for you to listen to, learn from, and laugh with. Come, hear the stories behind the poems and the poems behind the stories.  About Alt Poetry:Alt Poetry is a multi-channel poetry platform that brings poets, readers, and poetry lovers together to read, discover, and debate poetry from all around the world. We host different events online and in-person, including ‘Poet of the Month’, ‘Book Talk’, ‘Poetry Atlas ’, and ‘Poetry Classroom’.Alt Poetry is founded by Namratha Varadharajan (Author: On Cultivating Loudspeakers and Quilts -forthcoming from Booksthakam), Madhuri Katti (Author: Life, Time, and Other Things), and Rajani Radhakrishnan (Author: Water to Water, Duplicity, and No Way Home)Limited spots available.

name: GFT: November Edition in Bangalore
description: Grounds for Thought: Bangalore, November 2026A Blue Tokai × unLecture Series, Three evenings. Three very different conversations. Grounds for Thought brings researchers, scientists, and thinkers out of their institutions and into rooms full of curious people, where the conversation goes somewhere a classroom rarely does. This November in Bangalore runs from constitutional literacy to the history of economic ideas, closing with a reframing of how India's princely states shaped its founding.15th November: Anjor BhaskarDemocracy is declining around the world, Why don't young people care?Democracy doesn't die when constitutions fail — it dies when citizens stop practising democratic values. Anjor Bhaskar, faculty at Azim Premji University and founder of Dialogues on Democracy and Development, has worked with over 30,000 participants across India on what he calls constitutional literacy: translating values like liberty, equality, and fraternity into everyday practice. This session asks why so many young people know more about celebrities than the Constitution, why misinformation outruns truth so easily, and why constitutional morality may be the most important skill nobody is teaching.21st November: Alex M. ThomasFantastic Economic Theories and Where to Find Them Are wages and interest rates "fantastic" in the sense of excellent — or in the sense of hard to believe? Alex M. Thomas, Associate Professor of Economics at Azim Premji University and author of the widely used textbook Macroeconomics: An Introduction, takes this question through the history of economic ideas: does raising the minimum wage really raise unemployment? Does the rate of interest actually capture how people value the present over the future? An interactive session that moves from classical political economy to a sharper way of thinking about economic policy — and who it's really for.28th November: Shruti ViswanathanPrincely States and Constitutionalism: Uncovering the Many Imaginations of People, Power and Politics India's founding is usually told as a story with two actors — British India, and from 1946, the Constituent Assembly. Shruti Viswanathan, founder of The Equals Project and a graduate of NLSIU Bangalore and the Fletcher School at Tufts, argues that leaves out a third: the roughly 565 princely states governing a third of the subcontinent's population, usually mentioned only at the moment of their accession, as a problem to be solved rather than as sites of constitutional thought in their own right. This session reframes their integration as a provocation — revealing that the "Idea of India" was never a single, inevitable outcome, but a fiercely contested space with constitutional activity of its own, often well before 1947.

This November in Bangalore runs from constitutional literacy to the history of economic ideas, closing with a reframing of how India's princely states shaped its founding.15th November: Anjor BhaskarDemocracy is declining around the world, Why don't young people care?Democracy doesn't die when constitutions fail — it dies when citizens stop practising democratic values. Anjor Bhaskar, faculty at Azim Premji University and founder of Dialogues on Democracy and Development, has worked with over 30,000 participants across India on what he calls constitutional literacy: translating values like liberty, equality, and fraternity into everyday practice. This session asks why so many young people know more about celebrities than the Constitution, why misinformation outruns truth so easily, and why constitutional morality may be the most important skill nobody is teaching.21st November: Alex M. ThomasFantastic Economic Theories and Where to Find Them Are wages and interest rates "fantastic" in the sense of excellent — or in the sense of hard to believe? Alex M. Thomas, Associate Professor of Economics at Azim Premji University and author of the widely used textbook Macroeconomics: An Introduction, takes this question through the history of economic ideas: does raising the minimum wage really raise unemployment? Does the rate of interest actually capture how people value the present over the future? An interactive session that moves from classical political economy to a sharper way of thinking about economic policy — and who it's really for.28th November: Shruti ViswanathanPrincely States and Constitutionalism: Uncovering the Many Imaginations of People, Power and Politics India's founding is usually told as a story with two actors — British India, and from 1946, the Constituent Assembly. Shruti Viswanathan, founder of The Equals Project and a graduate of NLSIU Bangalore and the Fletcher School at Tufts, argues that leaves out a third: the roughly 565 princely states governing a third of the subcontinent's population, usually mentioned only at the moment of their accession, as a problem to be solved rather than as sites of constitutional thought in their own right. This session reframes their integration as a provocation — revealing that the "Idea of India" was never a single, inevitable outcome, but a fiercely contested space with constitutional activity of its own, often well before 1947.

name: Word of Mouth: A Food Walk with Berty Ashley
description: Have you ever stopped mid-bite and wondered why the thing you’re eating is called what it’s called? Why a galouti kebab is a galouti kebab, or which beloved drink took its name from a famously busty actress?Join quiz master Berty Ashley for an afternoon of eating through the city with a historian’s curiosity and a trivia-lover’s glee. As you wander, Berty unpacks the etymology and backstory behind iconic dishes: the accidents, empires, puns and personalities buried in names we say without thinking.The walk pans out on Church Street, hopping through some yummy spots including Indian Coffee House, Empire & Big Fat Roll.Berty AshleyBerty Ashley is a molecular biologist by day and one of Bengaluru’s best-loved quiz masters. He sets The Hindu’s weekly “Easy Like Sunday Morning” quiz, has co-authored a science quiz book, and is a serial collector of music, trivia and clearly food facts. Few people can make you this hungry and this much smarter in a single afternoon.Urbanaut ProductionsWe find the best a city has to offer and then we build a way in. Urbanaut Productions curates urban experiences at the intersection of food, art, music, and culture. For the curious, the restless, and anyone who suspects their city still has a few secrets left.
